warmup.q: The payments are split over 8 machines by the time each payment was made. Each machine holds one stretch of time, and together the stretches cover every possible time. They were chosen so that each machine got the same number of this morning's payments. This afternoon, 10,000 new payments arrive. How many land on the busiest machine?
options: About 1,250: the morning was split evenly, so the eight machines share the afternoon
About 2,500: the machines with the latest stretches are a little busier
All 10,000: every new payment is later than every payment already stored
It depends on how well the payments get mixed before they're placed
warmup.why: Each machine holds one unbroken stretch of time, and the last stretch runs from its start to the end of time. Every afternoon payment was made after every payment already stored, so each one falls into that last stretch, on the last machine. The demo in the second section counts [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 10000]. The first option is the tempting one, because the morning really was split evenly. But the stretches were cut from the morning's times, and the whole afternoon lies past them. The last option describes hashing, the third section's idea: nothing here mixes the payments.

sections.h: Copies can't make the data smaller, so we cut it into shards
sections.html:
Let's put numbers on the café's bad day. The payments table holds 3 billion payments. Each takes about 1 KB on disk, counting the indexes, the lookup lists that find a payment fast, so that's 3 TB. Every day adds 40 million payments, or 40 GB. The machine has 4 TB of disk, so the last free terabyte lasts 25 days.

The Replication track set this machine up as the leader. The leader takes every write, a request that stores or changes data, and sends it on to its followers, the machines that keep copies. Three followers can answer three times as many reads as the leader alone. They do nothing for the other two limits. Every copy stores all 3 TB. And every copy applies every write, so if the leader can't keep up with 25,000 new payments a second at the busiest moment, its followers can't either.

The fix is to split the data. Picture a parcel depot. One sorting bay can hold only so many parcels, so the depot has eight bays with a van for each, and every parcel goes into exactly one bay. We'll do the same with payments: cut the rows into parts, and put each part on a different machine. Each part is a shard. It holds some of the rows, and every row belongs to exactly one shard. With 8 shards, each holds about 375 GB and takes about an eighth of the writes. Stores give shards other names, such as partition, range, chunk or tablet, and this course says shard or partition. (A shard has nothing to do with a network partition, a break in the network that cuts machines off from each other.)

Sharding and replication work together. Each shard gets its own leader and followers, as in the Replication track. So one machine, or node, holds several shards, leading some and following others. A group of nodes that work as one store is called a cluster. When a node dies, followers on other nodes take over the shards it led.

So a sharded store keeps two maps, as the figure shows. The first takes a row's partition key to a shard. The partition key is the field, or fields, that decide where a row lives, such as the payment's number or the shop's id. The second map takes a shard to the nodes that hold its copies. This lesson is about the first map. Rebalancing and request routing, lesson 3 of this track, is about the second.

The first map has one more job: it must spread the work. If some shards hold more data or get more requests than others, the split is skewed. One shard with far more load than the rest is a hot spot, like one bay piled to the ceiling while seven vans wait. Skew eats the gain. Say one shard of eight takes half the writes. It reaches one machine's limit when the whole cluster is doing only twice one machine's work, and the other seven mostly wait.

Sharding has costs, so it isn't the first thing to reach for. A question that needs rows from several shards has to ask several machines. A change that must update rows on two shards together needs the machines to coordinate, which the Transactions track covers. And it's hard to change later. Figma, a company that makes a design tool people use in the browser, needed about nine months to move its first table onto shards. At the switch, some requests failed for about ten seconds.

Copies multiply the reads. Only splitting shrinks the data and the writes. So shard when one machine runs out of disk or of write speed. Next, we'll choose the first map, starting with the simplest one.

aside.title: Why not buy a bigger machine?
aside.html: You should, first. A bigger machine needs no new code, and Growing past one machine: shared-nothing, shared-disk and the cloud showed that you can now rent one with nearly 2,000 processor threads and 32 TiB of memory. But the price grows faster than the size, and there is a biggest machine. However big it is, every write still goes through that one machine. Sharding is what you do when the biggest sensible machine isn't enough, or won't be in a year.

sections.h: Key ranges keep neighbours together, and pile new payments onto the last shard
sections.html:
The depot's first idea is to sort by postcode. Bay 0 takes the postcodes from the start of the list up to one boundary, bay 1 takes the next stretch, and so on. A driver who delivers to one street finds all its parcels in one bay.

Let's do the same with keys. A key is the value we look a row up by. Keep the keys in sorted order, and give each shard one unbroken stretch of them. With account numbers as the key, shard 0 holds A-0000 up to A-2499, shard 1 holds A-2500 up to A-4999, and so on. The router, the bit of code that sends each request to its shard, keeps the sorted list of boundaries: three strings for four shards. To place a key, it runs a binary search. It compares the key with the middle boundary, throws away the half that can't hold it, and repeats. Even 100,000 shards take only 17 comparisons. That's key-range sharding.

Its strength is the range scan, a read of every key between two values, in order. Keys stay sorted inside a shard, and neighbouring keys share a shard. The code calls a shop a merchant, so shop ids start with M-. Build the key from the shop's id, the time and the payment's number, joined by #, like M-0042#09:15:03#pay-81701. Then all of shop M-0042's payments for one day form one unbroken run. "M-0042's payments since 09:00" goes to one shard (two, if the run crosses a boundary) and reads its rows in order.

Where should the boundaries go? Not at fixed points, because keys aren't spread evenly: shop ids starting with M-00 might be a third of all rows. So the store takes the boundaries from the data. It sorts a sample of keys and cuts it into equal runs, then splits any shard that grows too big. MongoDB, a popular database program that stores records as documents, works in ranges of 128 MB. Lesson 3 covers splitting; in this lesson the boundaries are given. Here the depot picture breaks: a depot can repaint its bay labels overnight, while moving a boundary between machines means copying their rows across the network.

The weakness is any key that grows over time: a timestamp (the moment a row was made), or an id that counts up by one for each new row. Each new value is bigger than every old one, so it falls past the last boundary onto the last shard. Every insert, every new row, goes to one machine while the others wait. The stepper shows it, and shows why splitting doesn't help. The store splits the busy shard, and its upper half becomes the new last shard, which takes every insert. MongoDB's manual warns about exactly this: with a key that only grows, the last range gets most of the writes.

This one hides well in testing. Load a year of old payments in one go, and they spread nicely over the shards, because the boundaries were cut to fit them. The trouble starts with live traffic, when every payment is the newest one.

The fix is to put something before the time. With the key shop#time, the afternoon's payments come from all the shops, so they land in all the shops' ranges, on every shard. You pay on another question. "Every payment from 14:00 to 14:05", across all shops, is now a small run inside each shop's range, on every shard. Whatever comes first in the key decides where new rows land. Choose it from the question that must be cheap.

The shop-first key spreads new payments only because they happen to come from many shops. Next, we'll spread keys whatever they look like.

try.title: Cut range shards from the morning, then insert the afternoon
steps: Read RangeShardsDemo.kt below. It makes 20,000 morning payments and cuts 8 range shards from their keys, so each shard holds 2,500 of them. Then it adds 10,000 afternoon payments and counts where they land. It does all this twice: once with the time first in the key, once with the shop first. No Docker needed.
Predict the afternoon's count for each shard, with each key. Which key makes "14:00 to 14:05" cheap, and which makes "M-0042's day" cheap?

code.title: RangeShardsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l01.demo import java.util.Random /** A payment on virtual time: milliseconds since midnight, no clock involved. */ data class Pay(val id: String, val merchant: String, val atMillis: Long) fun payments(count: Int, startMillis: Long, everyMillis: Long, firstId: Int, seed: Long): List<Pay> { val rnd = Random(seed) return (0 until count).map { i -> Pay("pay-${firstId + i}", "M-%04d".format(rnd.nextInt(500)), startMillis + i * everyMillis) } } fun hours(h: Int, m: Int = 0) = (h * 60L + m) * 60_000L /** Key-range shards: sorted split points; a key belongs to the shard after the last boundary <= key. */ class Ranges(val boundaries: List<String>) { fun shardOf(key: String) = boundaries.count { it <= key } companion object { // cut a sample into equal runs, so the shards follow the data fun fromSample(keys: List<String>, n: Int) = keys.sorted().let { s -> Ranges((1 until n).map { s[it * s.size / n] }) } } } /** Eight range shards cut from the morning's keys. Then the afternoon arrives. Where do the inserts go? */ fun main() { val morning = payments(20_000, startMillis = hours(8), everyMillis = 1_000, firstId = 0, seed = 7) val afternoon = payments(10_000, startMillis = hours(14), everyMillis = 5, firstId = 20_000, seed = 8) val day = morning + afternoon val byTime = { p: Pay -> "%013d#%s".format(p.atMillis, p.id) } val byMerchant = { p: Pay -> "%s#%013d#%s".format(p.merchant, p.atMillis, p.id) } for ((name, key) in listOf("time first" to byTime, "merchant first" to byMerchant)) { val shards = Ranges.fromSample(morning.map(key), 8) val inserts = IntArray(8).also { c -> afternoon.forEach { c[shards.shardOf(key(it))]++ } } // which shards would a query have to ask? the ones that hold at least one matching payment fun shardsHolding(match: (Pay) -> Boolean) = day.filter(match).map { shards.shardOf(key(it)) }.toSortedSet() println("key = $name, for example ${key(afternoon[0])}") println(" afternoon inserts per shard: ${inserts.toList()}") println(" shards holding 14:00 to 14:05: ${shardsHolding { it.atMillis in hours(14) until hours(14, 5) }}") println(" shards holding M-0042's day: ${shardsHolding { it.merchant == "M-0042" }}") } }

try.expect:
key = time first, for example 0000050400000#pay-20000
  afternoon inserts per shard: [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 10000]
  shards holding 14:00 to 14:05:  [7]
  shards holding M-0042's day:    [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
key = merchant first, for example M-0364#0000050400000#pay-20000
  afternoon inserts per shard: [1251, 1329, 1240, 1235, 1211, 1278, 1178, 1278]
  shards holding 14:00 to 14:05:  [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
  shards holding M-0042's day:    [0]

The numbers are the same on every computer, because the payments come from a seeded random generator (one that gives the same "random" numbers on every run) on made-up times, not the clock. With time first, all 10,000 new payments go to shard 7, the last range, and a five-minute window sits on one shard. With the shop first, new payments spread from 1,178 to 1,329 per shard, and one shop's whole day sits on one shard, but a five-minute window touches all eight. Neither key is better. Each one makes a different question cheap.

sections.h: Hashing spreads the keys and scatters the ranges
sections.html:
The depot's second idea ignores the address. It sorts each parcel by the last digit of its tracking number. Every bay now fills at the same rate, whatever the address. But one street's parcels end up in every bay, so every van has to drive down that street.

A hash function does the same for keys. It's a formula that turns any text into a big number that looks random, and it gives the same number every time for the same text. pay-20000 and pay-20001 come out nowhere near each other. To pick a shard, divide the hash by N, the number of shards, and keep the remainder. That's written hash mod N. With 8 shards, A-1001 hashes to 1005131691884159963, which leaves remainder 3, so it lives on shard 3. That's hash sharding.

Keys that grow over time now spread evenly, because times a few milliseconds apart hash to unrelated numbers. In the Try it below, the 10,000 afternoon payments, keyed by time, land between 1,202 and 1,299 per shard.

The hash must give the same number in every program, on every machine, every day, or a payment stored today can't be found tomorrow. It doesn't need to be the kind of hash that protects passwords, only stable and well mixed. Cassandra, a database built to spread over many machines, uses one called Murmur3. The Dynamo paper, Amazon's 2007 design that the Data models track met, used MD5, which our demos use too. Java's built-in String.hashCode() is stable but mixes badly: pay-1, pay-2 and pay-3 give 106441804, 106441805 and 106441806, three numbers in a row. Object.hashCode() isn't even stable, because it can change each time the program runs.

What hashing gives up is the range scan over the partition key. "Every payment from 14:00 to 14:05" was one shard with range sharding. Now those payments are scattered, and the question asks all 8 shards, because nothing tells the router which ones it could skip.

Cassandra and DynamoDB, a database that Amazon runs for its customers, win part of it back with a key in two parts. The first part, the partition key, is hashed to choose the shard. The second part keeps rows sorted inside one partition (Cassandra calls it the clustering columns, DynamoDB the sort key). Make the shop the first part and the time the second. Then "M-0042's payments since 09:00" is one partition on one shard, read in order. Only a range across many shops is lost. Figma made this trade. It hashes its shard keys, such as the user's id and the file's id, because ids that count up would have made hot spots. In return, range scans over those keys got slower.

Real stores rarely use hash mod N itself, because of what happens the day N changes; lesson 3 counts the damage. Some cut the hash numbers into stretches that split like key ranges, as DynamoDB does. Cassandra gives each node 16 stretches on a ring of hash numbers, which is lesson 2.

Hashing has one blind spot: a single busy key. Every row with the same partition key lands on the same shard, whatever the hash. Partition by shop on Black Friday, the busiest shopping day of the year in many countries, and let M-0042 take every fifth payment. Its shard gets 3,094 of 10,000 new payments while the others get about 950 each. A hash spreads keys, not requests. Lesson 2 splits a busy key into several.

So far every key has been a payment or a shop, one of thousands. But each shop is also one of the company's customers. Next, we'll give a customer a shard of its own.

try.title: Hash the same payments, then add Black Friday
steps: Read HashShardsDemo.kt. It takes the range demo's afternoon payments, plus a Black Friday copy in which shop M-0042 takes every fifth payment. Each shard is md5(key) mod 8. It tries two partition keys: the time plus the payment's number, and the shop alone (with each shop's rows sorted by time inside its partition, as Cassandra would keep them).
Predict: with the shop as the partition key on Black Friday, how many of the 10,000 new payments does M-0042's shard get?
Run it from the labs folder. Then look at the last line, which prints String.hashCode() for three neighbouring keys.

code.title: HashShardsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l01.demo import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.security.MessageDigest import java.util.Random /** The first 8 bytes of MD5: the same number in every process, and neighbouring keys land far apart. */ fun md5(key: String): Long = ByteBuffer.wrap(MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5").digest(key.toByteArray())).long /** Hash sharding: shard = hash mod 8. Same payments as the range demo, plus a Black Friday afternoon. */ fun main() { val shardOf = { key: String -> Math.floorMod(md5(key), 8L).toInt() } val afternoon = payments(10_000, startMillis = hours(14), everyMillis = 5, firstId = 20_000, seed = 8) // Black Friday: the same afternoon, but M-0042 takes every fifth payment val blackFriday = afternoon.mapIndexed { i, p -> if (i % 5 == 0) p.copy(merchant = "M-0042") else p } val byTime = { p: Pay -> "%013d#%s".format(p.atMillis, p.id) } val byMerchant = { p: Pay -> p.merchant } // the partition key alone; rows sort by time inside it for ((name, key) in listOf("time + id" to byTime, "merchant" to byMerchant)) { fun inserts(day: List<Pay>) = IntArray(8).also { c -> day.forEach { c[shardOf(key(it))]++ } }.toList() fun shardsHolding(match: (Pay) -> Boolean) = blackFriday.filter(match).map { shardOf(key(it)) }.toSortedSet() println("partition key = $name") println(" normal afternoon, inserts per shard: ${inserts(afternoon)}") println(" Black Friday, inserts per shard: ${inserts(blackFriday)}") println(" shards holding 14:00 to 14:05: ${shardsHolding { it.atMillis in hours(14) until hours(14, 5) }}") println(" shards holding M-0042's day: ${shardsHolding { it.merchant == "M-0042" }}") } println("String.hashCode() of pay-1, pay-2, pay-3: ${listOf("pay-1", "pay-2", "pay-3").map { it.hashCode() }}") }

try.expect:
partition key = time + id
  normal afternoon, inserts per shard: [1248, 1223, 1202, 1229, 1277, 1264, 1299, 1258]
  Black Friday,     inserts per shard: [1248, 1223, 1202, 1229, 1277, 1264, 1299, 1258]
  shards holding 14:00 to 14:05:  [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
  shards holding M-0042's day:    [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
partition key = merchant
  normal afternoon, inserts per shard: [1173, 1307, 1397, 1195, 1167, 1379, 1024, 1358]
  Black Friday,     inserts per shard: [927, 1028, 1136, 969, 940, 1083, 823, 3094]
  shards holding 14:00 to 14:05:  [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
  shards holding M-0042's day:    [7]
String.hashCode() of pay-1, pay-2, pay-3: [106441804, 106441805, 106441806]

Hashing the time plus the payment's number spreads the payments almost perfectly, even on Black Friday, but every question has to ask all 8 shards. Hashing the shop keeps M-0042's day on one shard (shard 7), so on Black Friday shard 7 takes 3,094 new payments against about 950 for each of the others. Even the normal afternoon is uneven (1,024 to 1,397), because 500 shops over 8 shards don't average out as well as 10,000 payments do. The last line shows why String.hashCode() makes a poor shard hash: neighbouring keys get neighbouring numbers.

sections.h: A shard for each customer: tenants, and cells that share nothing
sections.html:
Look at who sends the requests. Nearly every request to the payments app is about one shop: its payments today, its refunds, its balance. A customer whose data is kept apart from other customers' data is called a tenant, and here every shop is one. Sharding by tenant puts each tenant's rows on one shard, either a shard of its own or one shared with other small tenants. In the depot, it's the big online shop that ships thousands of parcels a day and gets a bay and a van to itself.

Notion, an app for notes and shared documents, sharded its database this way. Every block in Notion (a paragraph, a to-do, a page) belongs to exactly one workspace, a team's shared space, and people almost always work inside one workspace. So the workspace's id became the partition key. Notion made 480 logical shards, shards as the app sees them, and put 15 of them on each of 32 machines running PostgreSQL, a free database program. Each logical shard is a schema, a named group of tables inside one database. At the daily peak, some machines passed 90% CPU: their processors were busy 90% of the time. So Notion moved the shards onto 96 machines with 5 each, and the peak fell to about 20%. The logical shards stayed at 480 throughout; lesson 3 explains why that number matters.

Sharding by tenant buys isolation, a wall between customers. A shop whose month-end report reads its whole history slows its own shard, not everyone's. A bug in an access check, the code that decides who may see what, is less likely to show one shop's payments to another when they live in separate databases. You can restore one shop from a backup without touching the others, and export or delete one shop's data when a privacy law asks for it. You can keep a shop's data in the country its law requires, and try a change to the table layout on one shop at a time.

A cell takes the same idea past the database. A cell is a complete copy of the whole app, its programs and its storage, serving a fixed group of tenants and sharing nothing with other cells. A thin router in front maps each tenant to its cell, by a hash or by a lookup table, and that router is the only shared part. AWS, Amazon's business that rents out computers, gives the arithmetic in its design guidance. With 10 cells, a failure inside one cell, such as a bad deploy (a new version of the program that turns out to be broken), leaves 90% of requests untouched. The share of requests that one failure can reach is its blast radius, here 10%. The same guidance says to cap each cell's size, grow by adding cells, and deploy to one cell at a time.

The catch is that tenants differ in size enormously. The Try it below sizes 1,000 shops on a Zipf curve, a common shape for popularity. The second biggest shop sends half as much as the biggest, the third a third, and the k-th biggest 1/k. The biggest sends 13.4% of all payments. Hash it onto 10 cells and it shares its cell with 97 other shops. It's their noisy neighbour: when it gets busy, all 97 slow down, and a bad deploy to that cell hits 17.9% of payments. Placement that knows the sizes gives the biggest shop a cell of its own and spreads the rest evenly.

Three problems stay open. A tenant too big for one shard has to be split inside itself, which brings back everything earlier in this lesson. Thousands of tiny tenants with a database each cost too much, so they share. And a feature that reads across tenants, such as a fraud model (a program that learns from all payments to spot suspicious ones), has to read every shard.

There's a bigger limit, too. Every scheme in this lesson assumed that the number of shards never changes, and it always does.

try.title: Place 1,000 merchants on 10 cells
steps: Read TenantCellsDemo.kt. It sizes 1,000 shops on a Zipf curve, 20,000 payments a second in all, and the code calls them tenants T-0001 to T-1000. It places them on 10 cells twice. First by a hash of the tenant's id. Then by size: a shop over 2,000 payments a second gets a cell alone, and the rest go, biggest first, onto the emptiest shared cell.
Predict: under hashing, how many other shops share the biggest shop's cell?

code.title: TenantCellsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l01.demo /** 1,000 merchants on 10 cells. Sizes follow a Zipf curve: the k-th biggest sends 1/k as much as the biggest. */ fun main() { val total = 20_000.0 // payments a second, all merchants together val harmonic = (1..1_000).sumOf { 1.0 / it } val merchants = (1..1_000).associate { k -> "T-%04d".format(k) to total / (k * harmonic) } val cells = 10 // the thin router's rule: hash the tenant id mod the cell count val byHash = merchants.keys.associateWith { Math.floorMod(md5(it), cells.toLong()).toInt() } // size-aware: tenants over 2,000 a second get a cell alone; the rest go biggest first to the emptiest shared cell val bySize = LinkedHashMap<String, Int>() val loads = DoubleArray(cells) var nextDedicated = 0 for ((id, rate) in merchants.entries.sortedByDescending { it.value }) { val cell = if (rate >= 2_000.0) nextDedicated++ else (nextDedicated until cells).minBy { loads[it] } bySize[id] = cell loads[cell] += rate } println("T-0001 alone sends %.0f payments a second, %.1f%% of all".format(merchants.getValue("T-0001"), merchants.getValue("T-0001") / total * 100)) for ((name, placement) in listOf("hash of tenant id" to byHash, "size-aware" to bySize)) { val perCell = DoubleArray(cells).also { l -> placement.forEach { (id, c) -> l[c] += merchants.getValue(id) } } val home = placement.getValue("T-0001") val neighbours = placement.count { (id, c) -> c == home && id != "T-0001" } println(name) println(" payments a second per cell: ${perCell.map { "%.0f".format(it) }}") println(" T-0001 is in cell $home with $neighbours other merchants") println(" a bad deploy to cell $home hits %.1f%% of payments; to the quietest cell, %.1f%%" .format(perCell[home] / total * 100, perCell.min() / total * 100)) } }

try.expect:
T-0001 alone sends 2672 payments a second, 13.4% of all
hash of tenant id
  payments a second per cell: [1457, 1337, 1286, 1914, 2205, 980, 3573, 2739, 2921, 1588]
  T-0001 is in cell 6 with 97 other merchants
  a bad deploy to cell 6 hits 17.9% of payments; to the quietest cell, 4.9%
size-aware
  payments a second per cell: [2672, 1926, 1926, 1926, 1926, 1923, 1926, 1926, 1926, 1923]
  T-0001 is in cell 0 with 0 other merchants
  a bad deploy to cell 0 hits 13.4% of payments; to the quietest cell, 9.6%

Hashing ignores size, so cell 6 carries T-0001 plus 97 others, 3,573 payments a second, against 980 in the quietest cell. Placing by size puts T-0001 alone and leaves the other nine cells within 3 payments a second of each other. The share of payments that one broken cell takes down, its blast radius, is now 9.6% to 13.4%, close to the 10% that 10 cells promise. The router still has to remember where T-0001 went, so a lookup table beats a plain hash once tenants differ this much.

refs.title: Herding elephants: lessons learned from sharding Postgres at Notion
AWS Well-Architected REL10-BP03: use bulkhead (cell-based) architectures

opening:
It's the busiest shopping day of the year. You tap your card at a café, and the reader thinks for four seconds before it beeps. Behind it, one database on one machine records the card payments of thousands of shops. Two more machines keep full copies.

That machine is stuck twice over. It can't store the 25,000 payments a second that are arriving. And its disk holds 3 TB, grows by 40 GB a day, and has one terabyte left.

The tempting fix worked last time: add a copy. Copies helped when too many people were reading. But every copy stores and writes every payment, so a fourth copy is one more full disk that writes no faster.

Concurrent writes: last write wins, version vectors and CRDTs ended the Replication track by asking what to do when the data no longer fits on one machine. In this lesson, we'll cut the payments into parts, one machine per part, and try three ways to choose a payment's part. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a card reader that took four seconds, because one machine stored every payment and its copies did the same. Shards cut the data and the writes into parts, and the key decides how well. Time first piles new payments onto one shard, and a busy shop stays on one shard whatever the hash.

Look at the number on your last receipt or online order. Does it count up, or start with the date? If a store kept orders in ranges of that number, today's would all land on one shard.

Next, we'll add a fifth machine to four, count the payments hash mod N makes move, and see how a ring of hash values moves far fewer.

worked.title: Choose a partition key for the payments table

steps.say: Start from the questions the app asks, and how often each one comes at the busiest moment, not from the table. The payments table has four. (AP stands for access pattern, one kind of request.)
steps.code:
AP1  store a new payment                    25,000 / s
AP2  get a payment by its number             40,000 / s
AP3  one shop's payments for a day              300 / s   (the shop's own screen)
AP4  every payment in the last 5 minutes       1 / min   (a fraud report)

steps.say: Try the creation time as a range key. AP4 is one shard, but AP1 sends all 25,000 new payments a second to the last shard. One node takes every write, so this fails on the busiest question. Strike it.
steps.code:
key = created_at (range)
AP1  every insert on the last shard          rejected
AP4  1 shard

steps.say: Try the payment's number, hashed, on 16 shards. AP1 and AP2 spread, and each request touches one shard. AP3 has to ask every shard: 300 shop screens a second on 16 shards is 4,800 shard requests a second. AP4 asks every shard too, but only once a minute, which is fine.
steps.code:
key = hash(payment_id)
AP1  spread, 1 shard each
AP2  1 shard
AP3  16 shards per request = 4,800 shard requests / s
AP4  16 shards, once a minute

steps.say: Try the shop's id, hashed, with the time as the sorted second part. AP3 becomes one partition, read in time order. AP2 now needs the shop as well, so put the shop's shard into the payment's number when you create it, or keep a small table from payment number to shop. AP1 spreads, except for shops big enough to be busy keys on their own: check the biggest against what one shard can write before you choose (lesson 2).
steps.code: // the partition key decides the shard; the second part sorts rows inside it data class LedgerKey(val merchantId: String, val createdAt: Instant, val paymentId: String) fun shardOf(k: LedgerKey, shards: Int): Int = Math.floorMod(stableHash(k.merchantId), shards.toLong()).toInt() // time is NOT hashed // AP3: every key of one merchant hashes the same way, so its day is one shard and one sorted run

steps.say: Write the decision down with its numbers, so the next person can see what the key gave up.
steps.code:
chosen: (hash(merchant_id), created_at, payment_id)
  AP1  spread; busy-key check needed for the top shops
  AP2  1 shard, via the shop's shard built into the number
  AP3  1 shard, rows in order
  AP4  every shard, once a minute (accepted)

lab.title: Build a range router and a hash router, then place tenants on cells
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. All 16 fail with NotImplementedError, Kotlin's error for code that isn't written yet. Workload.kt is done for you: it makes payments on made-up times from a seeded generator, so every number in the tests is exact.

In Sharding.kt, write RangeSharding.shardOf as a binary search for the number of boundaries at or below the key, then shardsForRange. The boundary test passes, and so does the property test, which uses jqwik (a testing library that tries many random inputs) to check 300 random keys against a plain count.
Write RangeSharding.fromSample and HashSharding.shardOf. Watch the test time-ordered keys send every new payment to the last range: it expects [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 10000].

Experiment: in a hot merchant stays hot whatever the hash, print skew(byMerchant). Then change HashSharding(8) to HashSharding(64) and run it again. The skew grows with more shards: M-0042's 2,000 payments stay on one shard, while the average shard's share shrinks.
hints: Binary search: start with lo = 0 and hi = boundaries.size. While lo < hi, look at mid. If boundaries[mid] <= key, the answer is above mid, so lo = mid + 1; otherwise hi = mid. Return lo.

shardsForRange: the first shard is shardOf(fromInclusive), and the last is the number of boundaries strictly below toExclusive. Return (first..last).toSet(), or an empty set when fromInclusive >= toExclusive.
fromSample: sample.toSortedSet().toList() sorts the sample and drops repeats. Boundary i (for i from 1 until shards) is sorted[i * sorted.size / shards].
Math.floorMod(stableHash(key), shardCount.toLong()).toInt(). The hash can be negative, and % on a negative number gives a negative shard; floorMod doesn't.

bySize: sort with compareByDescending<Tenant> { it.paymentsPerSecond }.thenBy { it.id }, split with partition { it.paymentsPerSecond >= dedicatedAt }, and keep a DoubleArray of loads for the shared cells. require(big.size < cells) gives the error the last test expects.

drill.title: Both routers from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write rangeShard(boundaries: List<String>, key: String): Int, a binary search in which a key equal to a boundary goes to the shard on its right. Then write hashShard(key: String, shards: Int): Int with a stable 64-bit hash. Finally, name one question each one makes cheap, and one it makes expensive.

answer.html: fun rangeShard(boundaries: List<String>, key: String): Int { var lo = 0 var hi = boundaries.size while (lo < hi) { val mid = (lo + hi) ushr 1 if (boundaries[mid] <= key) lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid // equal goes right } return lo // the number of boundaries <= key } fun hashShard(key: String, shards: Int): Int = Math.floorMod(stableHash(key), shards.toLong()).toInt() // stable across JVMs, never negative // range: a scan over neighbouring keys is cheap; a key that grows over time piles onto the last shard // hash: inserts spread whatever the key looks like; a range over the partition key asks every shard

recap: Copies multiply only the reads: every copy stores every row and applies every write. When one machine runs out of disk or of write speed, split the rows into shards, each row in exactly one shard, and give each shard its own copies.
A sharded store keeps two maps: partition key to shard (this lesson) and shard to the nodes holding its copies (lesson 3). Skew and hot spots are the first map's failures.

Key ranges keep neighbouring keys on one shard, so a range scan asks one shard. A key that grows over time, like a timestamp or an id that counts up, sends every new row to the last shard, and splitting only moves the hot spot along.

Hashing spreads keys whatever they look like, but a range over the partition key asks every shard. A hashed first part plus a sorted second part (Cassandra, DynamoDB) keeps ranges cheap inside one partition. No hash splits one busy key.
Sharding by tenant (Notion's 480 workspace shards) and cells put a wall between customers: a small blast radius, and restore or deletion one tenant at a time. Big tenants need placing by size.
The limit: every scheme here assumed the number of shards never changes. With hash mod N, adding one machine changes the answer for most keys.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to shard the payments table by key range on created_at, the time each payment was made, so that a report of last month's payments reads one shard. Explain what will happen to new payments, propose a key, and say what your key gives up.
explain.answer: Range sharding keeps keys sorted and gives each shard one stretch of them. Every new payment has a later created_at than every stored one, so it falls past the last boundary onto the last shard. All new payments go to one machine while the others sit idle. Splitting that shard doesn't help, because the upper half of the split becomes the new last shard. I'd make the shop's id the partition key, hashed, and keep created_at as the sorted second part of the key. New payments then spread over all the shards, and one shop's payments for any stretch of time are one sorted run on one shard, which is what the shop's own screen needs. What it gives up is a time range across all shops: last month's report and the five-minute fraud report now ask every shard. That's fine, because they run rarely, and a report that heavy belongs on a copy of the data built for analysis anyway. Before we commit, we should check the biggest shops against what one shard can write, because a hash can't split one busy key.

deeper.html:
The many names. Each product names its shards differently. Kafka calls them partitions, CockroachDB ranges, HBase regions, MongoDB chunks, and Bigtable, YugabyteDB and ScyllaDB tablets. In PostgreSQL, partitioning means splitting one table into parts on one server: dropping an old month gets cheap, but no machine is added. Sharding spreads the parts over servers.

Splits, and splitting early. HBase splits a region when its files pass 10 GiB, and CockroachDB splits a range at 512 MiB, or when it gets too busy. A new, empty table starts as one range, so every early write hits one shard until the first split. HBase and MongoDB let you pre-split: create the boundaries before you load the data.

Ids that start with the time. A MongoDB ObjectId and a UUIDv7 both put the time first, on purpose, so that new ids sort last. On range shards they behave exactly like timestamps.

Tablets. ScyllaDB, a database that speaks Cassandra's protocol (the language its clients use), has left the fixed ring behind. Since ScyllaDB 2025.1, new keyspaces (Cassandra's word for a database) use tablets by default. A tablet is a range of one table's hash numbers; tablets split as the table grows, merge as it shrinks, and a load balancer moves them between nodes.

Two stories from real companies. Notion's post on sharding Postgres explains why it routed requests in its own code instead of using the database's built-in table partitioning, and why it picked 480 shards rather than 512. Figma's post explains why it built its own proxy instead of moving to CockroachDB, TiDB, Spanner or Vitess. It groups the tables that share a shard key into colos, so queries that combine those tables, and changes that touch several of them at once, work as long as they stay within one key. It also sharded logically, with Postgres views (saved queries that look like tables) over one database, before it sharded physically.

Further reading. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 7 (now called Sharding; the first edition said Partitioning) has a section on sharding for multitenancy. It adds a quieter point: a schema change rolled out tenant by tenant lowers the risk, but is hard to make all-or-nothing.

Sharding inside one machine. Redis, VoltDB and FoundationDB run one program per processor core, each doing one thing at a time, and shard the keys between them, so the cores never wait for each other.
